title: Half-pi blanket shawl
subtitle: A large DK semicircle worked to full blanket depth — cosy and generous.
excerpt: A generous semicircular shawl in DK wool using the half-pi construction, worked through a sixth doubling section to create a deeper, heavier shawl that functions as a lap blanket. Wingspan approximately 180 cm, centre-back depth approximately 80 cm when blocked. About 700 g of DK yarn.
sourceNotes: The half-pi construction is Elizabeth Zimmermann's invention, published in Knitting Without Tears (1971), §Shawls. The extension to a sixth doubling section to create a deeper, heavier shawl is a natural application of the same formula, described by Zimmermann herself as suitable for a larger shawl or lap blanket.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 44 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Wingspan approximately 180 cm. Centre-back depth approximately 80 cm. Blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: Elizabeth Zimmermann's semicircular shawl formula: start with a small cast-on at the straight top edge and double the stitch count at logarithmically increasing row intervals (3, 6, 9, 18, 27, 36, ...). Each doubling represents one section; adding more sections makes a deeper shawl.

content.text: A generous semicircular shawl in DK wool using the
half-pi construction
through six doubling sections rather than five. Wingspan approximately 180 cm, centre-back depth approximately 80 cm. Large enough to use as a lap blanket.

The sixth section uses 36 plain rows between doubling rounds, following the same logarithmic schedule as the beginner half-pi (3, 6, 9, 18, 27 become 3, 6, 9, 18, 27, 36). Budget about 700 g (about 1,540 m / 1,680 yards) of DK wool.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: About 700 g (1,540 m / 1,680 yards) of DK-weight yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 100 cm or longer; a 120 cm needle is useful for the final sections

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. The half-pi formula is gauge-tolerant: at 20 stitches per 10 cm the wingspan will be approximately 198 cm; at 24 stitches per 10 cm it will be approximately 165 cm. If you prefer a specific wingspan, continue or stop plain rows after the final doubling round until the wingspan measures as desired.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast on and half-pi schedule
Cast on 9 stitches. Work the six-section half-pi schedule:
Section 1: 3 plain rows → Increase row 1 (9 → ~17 sts).
Section 2: 6 plain rows → Increase row 2 (~17 → ~33 sts).
Section 3: 9 plain rows → Increase row 3 (~33 → ~65 sts).
Section 4: 18 plain rows → Increase row 4 (~65 → ~129 sts).
Section 5: 27 plain rows → Increase row 5 (~129 → ~257 sts).
Section 6: 36 plain rows → Increase row 6 (~257 → ~513 sts).
After increase row 6, work plain rows until wingspan reaches 180 cm (approximately 18 to 27 more plain rows at gauge).
Increase row
Increase row: k1, *yo, k1; repeat from * to end. (Roughly doubles the stitch count.)
Bind off
Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off. At approximately 513+ stitches the bind-off will take approximately 45 minutes to complete.
Stitch count check-ins
After increase row 4: approximately 129 stitches. The shawl should lie flat. If the lower curved edge ripples, add 3 to 4 extra plain rows before increase row 5.
After increase row 6: approximately 513 stitches. Wingspan approximately 168 cm. The shawl is approaching the final size.
Common faults

Lower edge ruffling in section 6: at this weight and gauge, the 36-row section 6 may slightly over-cup in DK. If the edge ripples after increase row 6, work 4 additional plain rows before binding off without a further increase row.
Circular needle too short: after increase row 5 the stitch count exceeds 250 and a 100 cm needle may be too short. Switch to a 120 cm needle when the stitches become crowded.
Blocking
Soak in cool water, press out in towels. Block on a clean floor if the blocking mat is not large enough. Pin the straight top edge and pin the curved lower edge to the full 180 cm wingspan.
Care
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry. A large blanket shawl takes 48 hours to dry thoroughly.
What to try next
Work the same six-section schedule in a colour sequence: one colour per section. The six sections become six concentric arcs of colour radiating outward from the neck edge.
